children: By Alan Murray

The last two decades have been a tough slog for legacy media companies. Technology destroyed their monopoly on information and decimated their business models. Only a few have successfully navigated the disruption.

Dow Jones is one, now enjoying record growth and profits. In this week's episode of WSJ Leadership Institute Presents: Leaders , I sat down with Almar Latour, CEO of Dow Jones and publisher of The Wall Street Journal, for a conversation about how the company has managed to prosper amid media disruption, and how it plans to deal with a new wave of change from AI.

Needless to say, I can't claim impartiality on this one. I've spent most of my career at this company and now report directly to Almar. I've known him since he was 24 years old, when I hired him to be a news assistant in the Washington bureau of the Journal. I consider him a friend.

But my impartiality aside, I think you will be interested in his thoughts on how Dow Jones has prospered in this time of media disruption; why he believes it will continue to do so in the age of AI; how to maintain trust in media in a deeply polarized society; how as a journalist he learned the skills necessary to be CEO; and why he recently did a deep dive into Dante's "Divine Comedy."
You can watch on wsj.com, or listen on Apple or Spotify .
Separately...

Erle Norton here. Journal reporter Fabiana Negrin Ochoa's interview with Insilico co-CEO Alex Zhavoronkov is a great read because it's an example of a chief executive injecting reality into a sector filled with hype while still pointing out the promise of his product.

Here's the promise part: Patients treated with Insilico's investigational drug rentosertib for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, an age-related lung disease, showed a decline in their biological ages. The biggest decline was six years.
"Six years is very promising, right?" Zhavoronkov said.
Here's the reality: "But I can tell you that it will take us a decade to prove that it's antiaging-if it gets approved."
And for those who think AI, which Insilico uses to develop drugs, will soon lead to a doubling of lifespans? "Absolute nonsense."
He noted that no drug in 150 years of discovery has been clinically proven to extend lifespans. "Regardless of how rich you are...you cannot buy one year of life with a drug."
